papers.title: Influence of interindividual variability structures on implied priors and population predictions in pharmacogenetic models
papers.abstract: Interindividual variability (IIV) defines part of the prior distribution used in Bayesian parameter estimation. However, the dependence of model-implied priors on IIV and covariate model specifications is rarely examined explicitly. We evaluated empirical support for pooled versus phenotype-specific IIV structures and their consequences for predictive distributions in a CYP2D6-dependent population pharmacokinetic model. Four variants of a published codeine-metabolite model were independently re-estimated in NONMEM using data from 997 patients, combining continuous activity-score or categorical CYP2D6 parameterizations with pooled or phenotype-specific IIV. Distributions of morphine formation clearance were simulated in mrgsolve with 10,000 virtual individuals per phenotype and model. Two controlled 2 x 2 simulations isolated the effects of IIV variance structure within each parameterization. Phenotype-specific IIV improved model fit under both parameterizations ({Delta}OFV -448.57 and -44.27, respectively). The corresponding IIV variance estimates for poor metabolizers were 5.79 and 0.355. ETA variance shrinkage exceeded 90% in poor and ultrarapid metabolizers under both phenotype-specific IIV models. The four fitted models differed in the central tendency and dispersion of predicted morphine formation clearance. In controlled simulations, phenotype-specific IIV increased the coefficient of variation of morphine formation clearance in poor metabolizers approximately threefold under the continuous parameterization and by approximately 40% under the categorical parameterization. Both IIV estimates and their effects on population predictions depended on CYP2D6 parameterization. Importantly, improved model fit alone does not establish the biological validity of these distributions, and their implications for individual Bayesian posterior predictions remain to be evaluated.

papers.title: The Impact of Highly Effective Modulator Therapies on the ABCG5 ABCG8 Sterol Transporter and Hepatobiliary Function
papers.abstract: Sitosterolemia (STSL) is a monogenic, recessive disorder characterized by the accumulation of xenosterols in plasma and tissues. STSL is caused by mutations in either ABCG5 or ABCG8, genes that encode ABC half-transporters that form an obligate heterodimer (G5G8) that opposes sterol absorption and promotes biliary cholesterol secretion in the small intestine and liver, respectively. Like STSL, Cystic Fibrosis (CF) is caused by mutations in an ABC transporter, the CF transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR, ABCC7). Highly Effective Modulator Therapies (HEMT) are small molecule drugs used in combination to treat CF. HEMT modulate additional ABC transporters, suggesting they may interact with G5G8 to alter wild-type or mutant protein function. We established human hepatocyte cell lines expressing ABCG5 and ABCG8 and tested the effect of HEMT independently and in combination on G5G8 protein abundance, localization, and maturation. HEMT increase G5G8 abundance, induce the appearance of a high-molecular weight form of ABCG5, and redistribute ABCG8 intracellularly in cultured hepatocytes. However, HEMT failed to rescue maturation of STSL-causing mutants of either ABCG5 or ABCG8 in vitro. Finally, we examined the effect of HEMT on G5G8 and biliary cholesterol secretion in mice. In contrast to cultured hepatocytes, HEMT reduced Abcg5 and Abcg8 protein and biliary lipid secretion. HEMT treatment also promoted hepatic triglyceride accumulation and the expression of collagens, suggesting that HEMT may contribute to CF with Hepatobiliary Involvement (CFHBI) in patients.

papers.title: A Novel Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme 2 Fusion Protein Reduces Cardiotoxic Effects of Doxorubicin
papers.abstract: Background: Anthracyclines, such as doxorubicin, are a cornerstone of chemotherapy and are the first-line therapy for high-risk breast cancer. Doxorubicin, however, induces dose-dependent cardiotoxicity that can lead to acute and chronic heart failure. In clinical studies with serial measurement of left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), targeting the Renin-Angiotensin System (RAS) with angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors was effective in ? 40% of patients (responders), but in 45% of patients, there was no response in LVEF. As such, there is a critical need to find new cardioprotective strategies. We posited that efficacy is limited by sole inhibition of the Angiotensin-II Type 1 Receptor (AT1R) RAS arm without activation of the mas receptor (MasR) RAS arm. Methods: To address this issue, we used a novel engineered angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) fusion protein therapeutic, which possesses enhanced activity and substrate specificity compared to wild-type ACE2 and contains a human IgG Fc domain that increases circulation lifetime; this approach simultaneously attenuates AT1R activation and activates MasR. Results: Mice treated with this protein, known as ACE2dm-Fc, in conjunction with doxorubicin administration had increased longitudinal body weight gain and were protected from left ventricular dysfunction and cardiac remodeling compared to mice receiving doxorubicin alone. Additionally, bulk-tissue RNA sequencing identified gene expression correlates of heart function that distinguished mice receiving both ACE2dm-Fc and doxorubicin from those given only doxorubicin. Conclusions: Our results establish ACE2dm-Fc's potential as a novel treatment for doxorubicin-induced decline in LVEF.

papers.title: Pharmaceutical agent cetylpyridinium chloride modulates mitochondrial dynamics to enhance calcium-stimulated immune mast cell function
papers.abstract: The public is routinely exposed to quaternary ammonium compound cetylpyridinium chloride (CPC) through myriad personal care, food, and cleaning products. However, at exposure-relevant and non-cytotoxic doses, CPC exerts mitochondrial- and neurotoxicity, even crossing the blood brain barrier. Previously, our lab showed that CPC inhibits IgE-mediated mast cell function (degranulation) by hampering early tyrosine phosphorylation events and signaling of the lipid PIP2, though direct CPC effects on the downstream portion of the pathway remained unknown. We used Ca2+ ionophore to directly shuttle Ca2+ into RBL-2H3 mast cells, bypassing the upstream events of IgE-mediated signaling and modeling alternative mast cell activation modes. Unexpectedly, CPC causes powerful stimulation of mast cell signaling under inducement of signaling proximal to Ca2+ entry; thus, immune pathways alternative to the classic IgE-mediated pathway may be activated by this compound. This finding demonstrates that CPC inhibition of IgE-mediated mast cell signaling solely involves events upstream of Ca2+. CPC enhancement of Ca2+ ionophore-stimulated degranulation is dependent on energy status, perhaps a modification of hormesis. CPC mechanism of boosting Ca2+ ionophore-mediated degranulation is characterized by effects on Drp1 phosphorylation, mitochondrial fission, energization (increased mitochondrial membrane potential), and mitochondrial translocation, mediated by microtubules. This may be the first instance of a chemical amplifying mitotranslocation. This work links and clarifies connections between Drp1, mitochondrial fission/translocation, and degranulation in basic cell biology. This work expands understanding of CPC mitotoxic mechanisms, connecting to its immunomodulatory effects and suggesting impacts of other quaternary ammonium compounds, to ultimately aid consumers and regulators in decision-making.

papers.title: A hydrocarbon pheromone mediates ant group cohesion
papers.abstract: Social insect colonies are among the most cohesive groups in the animal kingdom, yet we know little about the signals and sensory mechanisms that underlie their collective unity. Here, we show that cuticular hydrocarbons (CHCs), low volatility compounds present on the insect body surface, play a central role in social cohesion in the clonal raider ant, Ooceraea biroi. CHCs are transferred from the body to the nest substrate, where they are sufficient to induce aggregation. Nest associated CHCs elicit aggregation across distinct O. biroi genotypes, indicating that they function as a species wide signal. In contrast, hydrocarbon mixtures from other ant species or synthetic hydrocarbons absent from the O. biroi cuticle do not elicit aggregation. We further show that behavioral responses to nest associated CHCs vary with age and physiological state and correlate with the ants' propensity to leave the nest. This suggests that variation in responses to CHCs contributes to age based division of labor and other behavioral dynamics in the colony. Finally, we show that aggregation is specifically mediated by 11,15 dimethylheptacosane, the most abundant component of the O. biroi CHC profile. Together, these findings identify a pheromone based mechanism underlying group formation and persistence, as well as division of labor in the clonal raider ant.

papers.title: Digital news consumption as an information foraging problem
papers.abstract: News feeds are digitally available all around us, yet the cognitive mechanisms by which we decide what to spend time on, and what to skip, are not well understood. We formulate digital news consumption as an information foraging problem. In this formulation, users move between news articles, formalized as information patches, exploited them like agents consuming food in a canonical patch foraging task. The switching time between news article can be seen as a navigational process that happens at a time akin to the travel time in the canonical patch foraging formalism. To unravel mechanisms determining news reading times, we fit an evidence-accumulation model separately to each of 2,820 readers of a Norwegian newspaper across 1.9 million reads. Reading times are described by accumulation from a variable starting point, in which readers arrive already partly informed. We also show that readers can be divided into two groups reflecting different behavioral patterns that we name: committed and conditional reflecting different distributions of the fitted evidence accumulation model parameters. Our study opens up the opportunity to study the detailed cognitive mechanisms underlying news consumption and our preliminary analysis show that our information foraging approach can be generalized to our types of digital media human interact with on a daily basis.

papers.title: High Throughput Screening Of FDA Approved Drugs As Potential Agonist Of Mu-Opioid Receptor
papers.abstract: The mu-opioid receptor (MOR) remains an important analgesic target, but the interpretation of ligand-directed signalling preferences requires discrimination between receptor-dependent responses and effects on downstream assay readouts. We screened a library of 1,875 drug compounds for inhibition of forskolin-stimulated cyclic AMP (cAMP) accumulation in Chinese hamster ovary cells expressing human MOR and a GloSensor reporter. Primary screening of compound mixtures identified 17 active wells containing 204 compounds. Deconvolution yielded nine initial hits, six of which produced interpretable concentration-response relationships: niclosamide, sanguinarine, hexachlorophene, ataluren, altrenogest and nitazoxanide. Five of the six showed maximal cAMP inhibition of 77-80% in the initial concentration-response experiment, compared with 81 +/- 6% for DAMGO; sanguinarine had a lower maximum (24 +/- 6%). All six were less potent than DAMGO. In antagonist experiments, 300 nM naloxone shifted DAMGO potency from 0.3 to 224 nM. Of the tested compounds, only altrenogest showed a statistically significant naloxone-associated shift (367 to 905 nM; P = 0.0117). Altrenogest produced no detectable beta-arrestin2 recruitment under the PathHunter assay conditions, whereas DAMGO produced a concentration-dependent response. Thus, most cAMP hits did not show evidence of naloxone-sensitive MOR activation, and altrenogest showed a limited but measurable antagonist-sensitive component. These results highlight the importance of orthogonal receptor-dependence testing before assigning MOR agonism or signalling bias to repurposing hits.

papers.title: M4 Muscarinic Receptor Positive Allosteric Modulation Reduces Repetitive Grooming in Male SAPAP3-/- Mice in a Sex-Dependent Manner
papers.abstract: Background and Purpose: Pathological repetitive behaviors in obsessive-compulsive disorder are linked with altered striatal circuitry, and current treatments show variable efficacy and common side effects. We investigated whether the M4 positive allosteric modulator VU0467154 (VU'154) reduces repetitive grooming in SAPAP3-/- mice, and whether M4 receptors expressed in the dorsomedial striatum (DMS) mediate this effect. Experimental Approach: Spontaneous behavior was quantified in male and female SAPAP3-/- mice and wild-type littermates using depth Motion Sequencing (MoSeq) after VU'154 treatment (0.1-3 mg/kg, i.p.). M4 receptors in the DMS were deleted using virally transduced Cre in SAPAP3-/- mice carrying floxed M4 alleles, and receptor deletion was validated by assessing striatal Chrm4 RNA expression. Key Results: SAPAP3-/- mice displayed excessive grooming, hypolocomotion, reduced rearing, and increased inactivity compared to littermate controls. VU'154 reduced grooming in SAPAP3-/- males at a dose that did not significantly affect other active behaviors, while females unexpectedly showed no comparable grooming reduction. Higher doses suppressed active behaviors, including grooming, across genotype and sex. Deletion of M4 from the DMS increased grooming in SAPAP3-/- males but did not prevent VU'154-mediated reductions in grooming. Conclusions and Implications: M4 receptor potentiation selectively reduces excessive grooming in male, but not female, SAPAP3-/- mice, revealing a sex-dependent drug response. M4 receptors in the DMS appear to contribute to baseline grooming regulation in males but were not required for VU'154 efficacy, suggesting that other M4 receptor populations underlie these effects. These findings suggest that sex may be an important consideration in developing M4-targeted treatments for repetitive behaviors.

papers.title: Dog Meets Man: Alloparenting and Affective Care within Co-Constructed Street Dog-Human Lifeworlds in Delhi, India
papers.abstract: Rapid urbanisation and largely unplanned development in Indian cities have been drawing increasing ethnographic attention in recent years. Even though other-than-human beings are an integral part of these spaces, the city is still most often understood from a human perspective. Simultaneously, nonhumans actively shape and reshape their environments through everyday behavioural choices - choices that are not only ecological, but also socioeconomic, and often influenced by their interactions and relationships with human beings. In this paper, we adopt a mixed-methods, etho-ethnographic approach to explore a curious case of other-than-human alloparenting within largely affective dog - lifeworlds in the Indian megapolis of Delhi. We focus on a triadic relationship between two co-territorial female street dogs -- Bhuri and Kali -- and a particular human caregiver -- Kishan -- that reveal how these two dogs, sharing the same territory within Gur Mandi, an informal settlement in north Delhi, adjust their allo/parenting behaviour in response to their independent social interactions with the human residents of the area. This more-than-human narrative suggests that street dogs are not merely passive inhabitants of the city, but sentient, affective participants, who shape urban life through their everyday interactions. Moreover, the counter-intuitive shifts that we observed in multibeing parenting behaviour reflect how human presence could configure short-term social interactions and the long-term relationships between nonhuman beings in their shared spaces.

papers.title: Ruthenium Coordination Architecture Redirects Imiquimod Antiviral Activity
papers.abstract: Immune agonists can reinforce antiviral defence, but therapeutic efficacy requires control over the magnitude and quality of the host response. Here we show that metal coordination can reprogramme the pharmacology of imiquimod, a clinically used TLR7 agonist. A series of Ru(II)-arene-imiquimod complexes identified the trinuclear compound 7 as a lead with activity against Herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2 (HSV-1 and HSV-2), including clinical isolates and antiviral-resistant strains. Compound 7 directly reduced HSV-1 infectivity and broadly suppressed viral protein accumulation in infected fibroblasts. In patient-derived human ectocervical organoids, it reduced epithelial infection and the recovery of infectious virus. Transcriptomic and proteomic profiling showed that 7 selectively restored infection-suppressed interferon-responsive and antiviral restriction programmes. Thus, Ru coordination does not simply enhance imiquimod activity but redirects its pharmacology, coupling virus-directed activity to restoration of epithelial antiviral defence. These findings establish a broader principle: coordination chemistry can engineer the response profile of immune-active anti-infective agents and expand the design space of host-directed antiviral therapeutics.

papers.title: Actionable, Motivating, and Not Beyond Question: Student Insights On AI-Enabled Feedback and Instructor AI Use
papers.abstract: Scientific writing helps students develop and communicate their understanding through practices such as constructing explanations and arguing from evidence, but its complexity often requires individualized feedback and guidance. This makes scientific writing a worthwhile context in which to study the effects of feedback augmentation with generative AI (genAI). Although emerging work demonstrates that genAI can support feedback generation, considerably less is known about how students experience and respond to AI-enabled feedback. At the same time, feedback research has identified characteristics students view as supportive, yet it remains unclear whether these insights apply to AI-enabled feedback. Accordingly, this qualitative study examines biology students' experiences and perceptions of feedback developed by their instructor with assistance from a custom genAI tool in an authentic learning context. Analysis of student team interviews developed three themes: students recognized characteristics of effective feedback, positive emotions encouraged intention to revise, and students accepted but critically evaluated instructor AI use. Together, the themes suggest that AI-enabled feedback supported revision through both its content and its influence on students' academic emotions, which contributed to more favorable views of instructor genAI use. However, students' evaluations also depended on whether AI use aligned with their expectations and on the credibility of both the instructor and the genAI tool, for which instructor oversight was an important consideration. Collectively, these findings highlight the importance of a learner-centered approach to genAI implementation that accounts for students' needs and expectations and promotes engagement with feedback. Together, these findings suggest that students' positive perceptions of AI-enabled feedback were rooted less in the use of AI itself and more in the extent to which the feedback supported revision and improvement.

papers.title: Interpreting citizen science data for larval surveillance: lessons from storm drain reports in Mosquito Alert
papers.abstract: Mosquito-borne diseases are an increasing public health concern, and urban drainage infrastructure such as storm drains and catch basins can provide breeding habitat for Aedes vectors, including Aedes albopictus. Detecting these sites over large areas is costly with traditional surveillance alone, and citizen science offers a complementary, lower-cost source of geolocated observations. Mosquito Alert is a citizen science platform, active since 2014, through which participants report adult mosquitoes, bites, and potential breeding sites. In this work, we present a descriptive analysis of the 17,880 storm drain breeding sites reported through the platform from June 2014 to August 2026, obtained from the project's public map. We counted the reported sites by country and geographic coordinate, examined when reports are submitted and which fields are recorded, estimated how often water and larvae are reported, and mapped the records globally. We also developed an interactive map to help inspect regions where many records overlap. Spain accounts for 90% of the records, 82% of all reports were submitted between April and June, and half of them fall on only 50 days. Group events, defined as five or more users reporting in the same municipality on the same day, account for 63% of the records. Water was reported in 43% of the storm drains: 33% in group events and 61% in the remaining reports. Larvae information exists for only 1,739 records; almost all are drains with water, and 28.5% of those had larvae, with higher shares in the warmer months and where participants noticed adult mosquitoes nearby. Our aim is not to model mosquito populations but to describe the structure of the data and highlight patterns worth further investigation. Because citizen science reporting effort varies across space, time, and socioeconomic groups, we discuss how sampling bias and other limitations of volunteer-based data affect the interpretation of these patterns and what they imply for the use of such data in larval surveillance.

papers.title: Detail: species-agnostic, generalizable animal behavior analysis using foundation model embeddings
papers.abstract: Automated tools for quantifying and classifying animal behavior from video data are crucial for neuroscience, medicine, and biology. Automated analysis of animal behavior from video usually starts with pose estimation, which needs manually annotated training frames for each new species or setup and reduces an animal to a small number of biased keypoints. Here we present Detail, a behavior analysis package built on foundation vision models, for species- and context-agnostic analysis of animal behavior. Animals are segmented from video frames using SAM 3, egocentrically aligned using keypoints placed by DINOv3 patch matching, and encoded by a frozen DINOv3 model as high-dimensional pose embeddings. Beyond a few annotated example frames, no labeled training data are required. Segmentation and keypoint models can be distilled into YOLO models that run quickly on a single consumer graphics card. Analysis modules operate directly on the pose embeddings for unsupervised behavior discovery, example-based behavior retrieval, precision auditing, and statistical comparison across experimental conditions. At the core of Detail is a pose embedding space, generated from an experiment's videos, that represents animal behavior. The complete workflow, from installation to analysis, is available through graphical and command-line interfaces for scripted and high-throughput use. Detail is available at https://github.com/detail-embedding/detail.

papers.title: pyMultiVideo: Open-source, Python-based, software for acquiring, synchronising, and compressing video from multiple cameras
papers.abstract: Video acquisition plays a critical role in many scientific experiments, enabling the quantification of human or animal behaviour, and movement of physical systems. Scientific applications place exacting demands on video acquisition, often requiring multiple cameras, high frame rates, synchronisation between cameras or with other hardware, control of camera parameters, and efficient data storage with comprehensive metadata. Here we present pyMultiVideo, an open-source Python application for scientific video acquisition. Features of the software include a graphical user interface (GUI) for efficiently configuring and running multi-camera experiments, online video compression using the computer's GPU, and synchronisation through recording GPIO pins states or external frame triggering. The code-base is simple and modular, with a separation of camera API from GUI code to facilitate adding support for additional camera systems. We outline the design and functionality of the software and present validation experiments demonstrating simultaneous recording and compression from multi-camera setups, at high frame rates without dropped frames on modest computer hardware.

papers.title: Model-based acoustic gaze inference for behaviour in the field, array design and honest uncertainty estimation
papers.abstract: Active sensing animals like echolocating bats and porpoises modulate their sensory volumes in a directed manner by altering various aspects (aim, beam width, source-level) of their calls or clicks, termed 'acoustic gaze'. Studying acoustic gaze requires inferring the beam parameters from a limited set of sensors, which is however a non-trivial task. To aid inference, studies apply a series of experimental constraints and data curation practices (e.g. animals always facing towards the array, only calls with peaks within X degrees of the centre analysed). Particularly for field studies, these constraints drastically reduce the volume of data, and remove important spatio-temporal context. Here I present a model-based Bayesian paradigm to perform acoustic gaze inference that releases the need for arbitrary constraints and curation practices such as animal flight direction or aim with three computational demonstrations 1) recovering acoustic gaze from a free-flying animal without constraints 2) post-hoc calibration of previously published array geometries that expand the spatial range of analysable calls and 3) a priori calibration of a proposed array design to avoid inefficient designs. The model-based paradigm expands the conditions under which acoustic gaze inference can be done, while also providing a principled approach to honestly estimate the uncertainty in estimated parameters.

papers.title: Nicotine stimulates chemosensory behavior and reduces aggression towards tobacco-feeding caterpillars (Manduca sexta) by predatory side-blotched lizards (Uta stansburiana)
papers.abstract: Herbivorous insects that feed on toxic plants have not only evolved to tolerate the chemical defenses of their hosts, but to co-opt them for their own defenses. Previous research has shown that the tobacco hornworm (Manduca sexta), a specialist herbivore of alkaloid-rich Solanaceous plants, is capable of exhaling ingested nicotine to defend itself from spiders; a phenomenon known as defensive halitosis. In this study, we aimed to uncover the effect of nicotine on interactions between predatory lizards (Uta stansburiana) and lepidopteran larvae (Manduca sexta and Spodoptera exigua). We leveraged transgenic lines of wild tobacco (Nicotiana attenuata) that are unable to produce nicotine or that inhibit M. sextas defensive halitosis via RNAi. We found that ingested nicotine in prey altered the rates of chemosensory and aggressive behaviors performed by lizards, yet there was no effect of inhibiting M. sextas ability to use ingested nicotine in a defensive halitosis. Furthermore, we found that nicotine had no effect on interactions between lizards and S. exigua larvae. These results suggest that nicotine on the surface of tobacco-feeding insects, but not volatile nicotine, influences lizard behavior in a dose-dependent manner rather than being a universally aversive chemical cue.

papers.title: Within-group disagreements delay collective movement decisions in wild birds and primates
papers.abstract: One of the benefits of shared decision-making is that it can resolve conflicting preferences among group members. This allows the members of moving animal groups to maintain cohesion while deciding on where to go next. However, followers are faced with decisions that vary in complexity. At some times followers only have a single initiator to choose from, while at other times they may have to select among multiple simultaneous initiators each moving in different directions. One question is whether increased disagreement, in terms of the number and spread of directions among initiators, has an impact on the time it takes for followers to make their move. Here I use whole-group GPS tracking datasets from vulturine guineafowl (Acryllium vulturinum) and olive baboons (Papio anubis) to link the complexity of the decision arising from disagreement to the time it takes for followers to resolve a movement decision. Across both species, there is a significant impact of having more initiating directions, with every additional direction adding approximately 11 s (for 1 direction) to 99 s (for 9 directions) on decision time. This suggests that both suffer from the paradox of choice. In vulturine guineafowl, high directional conflict also added up to 162 s on decision times relative to low direction conflict, whereas baboons appeared unaffected by directional conflict. Overall, these results confirm that within-group disagreement among initiators can increase the complexity of decisions faced by followers, and that this ultimately increases the time needed to resolve movement decisions.

papers.title: Structure-activity-guided design of potent and selective SSTR2 agonists inspired by a cone snail venom peptide
papers.abstract: The human somatostatin 2 receptor (SSTR2) is an important diagnostic and therapeutic target in neuroendocrine disorders and cancer. Because the endogenous peptide hormone somatostatin lacks in vivo stability and receptor subtype selectivity, significant effort has gone into the development of stable and selective peptide ligands such as octreotide and vapreotide. We recently identified Consomatin pG1, a somatostatin mimic from the venomous fish-hunting cone snail Conus geographus, that shares key stability-enhancing features with clinical somatostatin analogs, including a compact cyclic fold and a D-Trp residue, while exhibiting superior selectivity for SSTR2. Here, we define the structural basis of this selectivity by determining the cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of the pG1-human SSTR2-Gi3 complex at 1.9 angstrom resolution. Combined with receptor chimera and mutagenesis studies, these data reveal how pG1 engages the orthosteric binding site and forms critical interactions with extracellular loop (ECL) regions, notably ECL2. Guided by these insights, we designed a series of pG1 analogs with further enhanced potency, while retaining selectivity at SSTR2. Together, our findings offer insight into the molecular determinants of SSTR2 engagement and selectivity and provide new SSTR2-selective tool compounds and potential therapeutic leads.

papers.title: Use of orthogonal split inteins to direct surface expression of specific metabotropic glutamate receptor hererodimer pairs.
papers.abstract: Metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluRs) are class C G protein coupled receptors that function as obligate, covalently linked homo- and heterodimers in some combinations. The pharmacological responses of heterodimers to selective ligands are difficult to predict, and due to the tendency to homodimerize, heterodimers cannot be easily expressed in isolation. Here, we developed a split-intein-based approach to preferentially direct the plasma membrane expression of defined mGluR heterodimers, enabling their pharmacological characterization with minimal homodimer interference. Our strategy employs orthogonal split inteins flanking an endoplasmic reticulum retention/internalization sequence within the receptor C-terminal tail. Association of receptors carrying complementary intein modules promotes protein trans-splicing, removing the trafficking restriction and allowing receptor delivery to the cell surface. Following a systematic screening, the orthogonal Avi PRP8 and Mja KlbA inteins (designated C and F) were selected to generate complementary constructs. Co-expression of these constructs produced functional responses from multiple group II and III mGluR combinations, whereas individually expressed receptors generally lacked detectable signaling. Pharmacological characterization of mGlu2/4 using subtype-selective agonists supported the preferential expression of functional heterodimers over homodimers. Furthermore, glutamate dose-response profiles of most CF/FC receptor combinations closely resembled those obtained using the heterodimer-selective CODA-RET assay, supporting the ability of this approach to distinguish heterodimer-mediated signaling. Independent HiBiT-based surface-expression measurements confirmed partner-dependent membrane delivery while revealing receptor-specific limitations in retention efficiency, particularly for mGlu8-containing constructs. Together, these findings establish orthogonal split inteins as a tool for the selective functional and pharmacological characterization of mGluR heterodimers while minimizing interference from homodimer signaling.

papers.title: Assessment of dopaminergic neurotoxicity of CYP2E1-mediated trichloroethylene metabolites in C. elegans
papers.abstract: Trichloroethylene (TCE) is an industrial solvent associated with Parkinson's Disease (PD). Studies have demonstrated that TCE undergoes extensive metabolism in humans, suggesting that TCE toxicity may be attributable to its metabolites. However, knowledge of how TCE metabolites contribute to neurotoxicity in PD remains limited. We exposed Caenorhabditis elegans (C. elegans) to the TCE metabolites trichloroacetic acid (TCA) and trichloroethanol (TCEOH) to determine if exposure disrupts dopamine-dependent behaviors, such as movement and egg retention, and impairs dopamine neuron viability. TCA and TCEOH were selected because we have demonstrated that they are either detected or likely present in mouse brain after a human-relevant inhalation exposure to TCE. Wild-type, GFP-expressing, and an a-synuclein-expressing strain were exposed to 5 mM TCEOH, 10 mM TCA, or control doses. Dopaminergic neuronal viability and movement was assessed following 5 days of exposure and revealed a lack of pronounced neurodegeneration or deficits in movement following either exposure. However, TCEOH exposure for 2 days resulted in changes in egg retention, suggesting that it may disrupt dopaminergic or serotonergic neurotransmission. Although C. elegans-based assays can identify changes in PD-relevant outcomes, this study suggests that TCA and TCEOH in this exposure paradigm display limited morphological or behavioral toxicity in C. elegans, warranting further investigation of these metabolites in additional C. elegans and mammalian studies.

papers.title: Sucker recruitment patterns on the octopus arm during chemotactile exploration
papers.abstract: Octopuses possess highly flexible arms lined with chemo- and mechanosensory suckers that mediate exploration, prey capture, and object manipulation. How individual suckers communicate with adjacent and distant suckers to accomplish such tasks is poorly understood. We developed a behavioral protocol with Octopus bimaculoides to investigate inter-sucker recruitment once an individual sucker encountered an object of interest. We filmed the suckers on individual arms interacting with agarose disks embedded with prey extract and analyzed recruitment dynamics along the two longitudinal rows of suckers on each arm. We observed 18 recruitment patterns involving different sequences of ipsilateral and contralateral suckers. Octopuses most frequently recruited ipsilateral neighboring suckers along the same row, yet many patterns included contralateral suckers in diverse combinations. Recruitment occurred more rapidly toward the arm tip than toward the arm base, and local coordination was ultrafast (mean 155.9 ms between sucker attachments). This directionally organized, ipsilaterally biased, yet flexible recruitment is consistent with distributed neural control along the octopus arm, which may allow octopuses to adapt sucker coordination to the demands of manipulating different items, and may inspire innovation in sucker arrangement and coordination in soft robotic arms.

papers.title: Relying on a declarative as opposed to a procedural learning strategy predisposes to the development of instrumental habits in female but not in male rats
papers.abstract: Across species, individuals differ in their reliance on declarative versus procedural long-term memory systems for exploring and controlling the environment, mapping respectively onto allocentric place versus egocentric response learning strategies in a spatial navigation task. Several factors motivate the widely held consideration that procedural spatial learning strategies are generalisable to stimulus-response habits in the domain of instrumental conditioning, and vice versa; however, this hypothesis has received little empirical testing. Here, in a prospective longitudinal study of 72 rats (36 females), each animal was characterised for its place/response learning tendency using a dual-solution T-maze task and a 'direct opposition' test. Rats were then instrumentally conditioned to lever-press for food under a variable interval (VI) 60s schedule of reinforcement for five (Experiment 1) or 20 (Experiment 2) daily sessions, and the associative nature of their responding was assessed via sensitivity to offline reinforcer devaluation by pre-feeding to satiety. Against our hypothesis, response learners were less prone than place learners to rely on stimulus-response habits, an effect confined to female rats. Taken together, these findings reveal a complex, sex-dependent relationship between declarative and procedural memory systems and the two-fold associative basis of instrumental behaviour.

papers.title: A scalable method for preparation and long-term preservation of tea leaf plant-derived vesicles in tissue regeneration and drug encapsulation
papers.abstract: Plant-derived vesicles (PDVs) are emerging as sustainable nanotherapeutic platforms, although challenges regarding isolation, scalability, biological activity, drug loading, and storage stability hinder their biomedical translation. This study aimed to optimize PDV production, exploring different sources to assess the one with greater translation potential, in terms of for yield and purity. To that end, PDVs from tea and red cabbage leaves, as well as ginger and turmeric roots were isolated by differential ultracentrifugation and size-exclusion chromatography (SEC), comparing both methodologies. Tea provided the highest vesicle yield and purity, with SEC outperforming ultracentrifugation in reducing soluble protein contamination. SEC isolated tea leaf-derived PDVs (Tea PDVs) were therefore further optimization using scalable fast protein liquid chromatography. Proteomic characterization showed enrichment in hydrolases, which could be related to an inherent capacity to induce tissue remodelling. Hence, regenerative potential was tested in vitro on mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) and endothelial cells (HAECs). Firstly, Tea PDVs showed no cytotoxicity in MSCs and HAECs, even at high concentrations. Importantly, they significantly attenuated staurosporine-induced MSC death and promoted endothelial wound closure and capillary-like network formation, supporting their regenerative potential. Drug delivery potential was also assayed using quercetin, as a proof-of-concept drug. Saponin-mediated permeabilization significantly improved quercetin loading compared with passive incubation. Another important hurdle towards clinical translation, is determination of the ideal storage conditions for PDVs, which is still missing. To address this, we performed a six-months storage study at -80 C, analysing different cryopreservatives. The results showed that PBS alone caused substantial particle loss and increased vesicle size, whereas HEPES + trehalose-, sucrose-, and trehalose + human albumin-containing cryoprotective formulations preserved vesicle size and mitigated particle loss, facilitating long-term stability. Overall, these findings identify Tea PDVs as promising biocompatible nanocarriers with intrinsic regenerative properties. The optimized isolation, drug-loading, and preservation strategies provide a foundation for further development of plant-based nanotherapeutics targeting tissue regeneration and drug delivery applications in regenerative medicine.

papers.title: CLOVER: Chemical-gene LLM benchmark for obtaining valid entity relationships for the Comparative Toxicogenomics Database (CTD)
papers.abstract: Objective: The Comparative Toxicogenomics Database (CTD) provides expert-curated chemical-gene interactions about environmental exposure effects on human diseases. Existing automated relation extraction systems are typically restricted to 3-10 interaction types and operate on abstracts only. We introduce CLOVER, a systematic benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) on full-text chemical-gene interaction extraction using CTD-defined chemical-gene interaction terminology. The framework is designed to support 47 base interactions with directional modifiers (increase, decrease, affects), yielding 136 possible supported interaction classes. Evaluation is restricted to the subset of classes represented in the selected articles. Methods: CLOVER processes 50 full-text PubMed Central articles (1,563 sections) with PubTator and CTD integration. The pipeline consists of four stages: (1) LLM Extraction with one-shot and few-shot prompting; (2) LLM Validation to confirm and revise interactions; (3) Rule-based Refinement of extracted interactions to standardize terminology and eliminate errors; and (4) Human Review for expert oversight. We benchmark four LLMs (GPT-4.1, GPT-4o, Claude-Sonnet-4.5, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash) and compare against a naive baseline that applies unstructured prompting directly to full-text PDFs. Results: The naive baseline achieves only 13% recall and 36% precision. Refinement significantly enhances performance by eliminating unsupported interactions. Under strict limitations, Claude-Sonnet-4.5 alone achieves 72% recall and 61% precision, and Claude with self-validation achieves 74% recall and 49% precision compared to CTD. Of the 136 supported interaction classes, 17 were represented in our evaluation. Conclusion: To our knowledge, CLOVER establishes the first benchmark for full-text chemical-gene interaction extraction aligned with CTD. Our findings demonstrate that CLOVER achieves workable metrics for CTD-aligned curation relative to minimal whole-PDF prompting. This study addresses only a fraction of the content manually curated in CTD; considerably more work is needed to advance LLM-based tools to determine the extent to which these tools can approximate the full capacity of manual curation at CTD.

papers.title: Oral Silver Nanoparticle Exposure Increases Phosphorylated Tau Protein and Antioxidant Expression in Dentate Gyrus of Rat Brain
papers.abstract: Silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) are incorporated into products including toys, cosmetics, and surgical tools due to their antimicrobial properties. AgNPs can cross the blood-brain barrier and bioaccumulate in the brain, persisting for months with no clearance. We previously found that AgNPs disrupt the f-actin cytoskeleton, induce neurite collapse, and disrupt cytoskeletal regulatory pathways in cultured neural cells. The cytoskeleton is critical to maintaining synaptic structure and mediating neuroplasticity, therefore we investigated if AgNPs induce nuclear accumulation of hyperphosphorylated tau (ptau) and superoxide dismutase-1 (SOD1) in the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus to further assess nano-bio interactions in the brain. Following nine weekdays of treatment with 0, 25, or 100 mg/kg oral AgNPs, brains were collected one day after treatment to measure acute effects or one month post-treatment to measure the effect of bioaccumulated AgNPs. Using immunohistochemistry, we determined that ptau aggregates and SOD1 expression were significantly increased in the dentate gyrus after acute exposure and remained significantly elevated after exposure to bioaccumulated AgNPs. These findings suggest that exposure to AgNPs induces persistent disruptions to cytoskeletal regulatory proteins and antioxidant mechanisms associated with neurogenerative disease. Acute AgNPs exposure also induced minor disruptions in neurogenesis in the subventricular zone - rostral migratory stream - olfactory bulb niche that was reversed in rats exposed to bioaccumulated AgNPs. As AgNPs continue to be incorporated into everyday products, these data emphasize the importance of investigating their effect on mechanisms that may increase the risk of neurodegenerative diseases.

papers.title: DYRK1A inhibition by the postbiotic metabolite Urolithin A contributes to enhanced β-cell function: Structural, Biochemical and Cellular Evidence
papers.abstract: Urolithin A (UA), a postbiotic metabolite of ellagitannins (ETs), has shown potential in modulating metabolic disorders but the mechanisms underlying these activities remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigate the influence of UA on {beta}-cell function and assess the role of dual-specificity tyrosine-regulated kinase 1A (DYRK1A) inhibition in mediating these effects. We develop a novel transition-metal-free synthesis of UA employing a one-pot triple Baeyer-Villiger oxidation. Biophysical and biochemical analyses demonstrate that UA, and to a lesser extent its glucuronides (UA 3/8-gluc), bind to and inhibit DYRK1A, whereas the dietary precursor ellagic acid (EA) is inactive. Cellular studies confirm the intracellular DYRK1A engagement by UA but not by UA 3/8-gluc. To elucidate the molecular basis of this inhibition, we solve the crystal structure of UA-DYRK1A complex, providing the first high-resolution structural data on UA binding to a protein target and explaining the differential activities of UA, UA 3/8-gluc, and EA. Studies in MIN6 cells show that UA enhance glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (GSIS) and increase cell proliferation to levels comparable with the potent DYRK1A inhibitor harmine. These findings propose a new mechanistic link between postbiotic metabolites of ETs and insulin homeostasis and establish a structural basis for development of urolithin-based kinase inhibitors.

papers.title: Drosophila dormancy independently regulates huddling and aggregation site selection
papers.abstract: Dormancy is a reversible physiological state characterized by attenuated metabolism, reproduction, and feeding, yet the behavioral adaptations accompanying this state remain poorly understood. Here, we show that cold-induced dormancy in Drosophila melanogaster promotes the formation of large huddles ([≥]5 flies), which are rarely observed under warm conditions. Dormancy simultaneously shifts these huddles away from food, though the increased propensity to huddle persists even in the absence of food, revealing separable changes in huddling propensity and aggregation site selection. We further show that dormancy resets appetite, suppressing feeding despite energetic need. Neither starvation, unrestricted feeding, nor refeeding after starvation under warm conditions reproduced the dormancy-associated pattern of aggregation, suggesting that appetite suppression during dormancy extends beyond the range of normal warm hunger and satiety states. Increasing appetitive drive during dormancy nevertheless redirected aggregation toward food. A screen of appetite-regulating neuropeptide pathways identified Neuropeptide F (NPF) signaling as a regulator of both feeding and huddling during dormancy. Broad NPF activation increased feeding and suppressed huddling, whereas activation of an NPF-expressing fan-shaped body sub-population suppressed huddling without increasing feeding. Together, these findings establish huddling as a behavioral hallmark of Drosophila dormancy and demonstrate that the propensity to huddle can be experimentally dissociated from appetite-dependent aggregation site selection.

papers.title: Evidence for correlated evolution of sleep architecture in chronotype populations of Drosophila melanogaster created by artificial selection
papers.abstract: Chronotypes are circadian variants in timing of a behaviour. In humans, some studies have associated differences in sleep timing and quality with underlying circadian clock driven chronotypes although confounding genetic, environmental and social factors complicate the interpretation of these relationships. Here, we present evidence from artificially selected early and late eclosion chronotype populations of Drosophila melanogaster which suggest that divergence in chronotype can lead to correlated evolution of changes in sleep architecture. We find that early chronotype flies exhibit greater sleep fragmentation and shorter sleep latency during night, whereas late flies showed weaker and less consistent changes in the same direction. These differences were broadly seen for both sexes. We also show that environmental cues like temperature cycles can modulate sleep timing and enhance chronotype differences, while increasing light intensity delayed nighttime sleep timing similarly across chronotypes. Additionally, when sleep was disrupted by mechanical perturbations, late flies could not recover lost sleep to the same degree as early and control in a time-of-day dependent manner. In contrast, following simulated jetlag-induced circadian misalignment, early flies showed a greater increase in daytime sleep after phase advances. Our findings suggest that sleep and circadian traits can coevolve, offering insights into the complex interactions between chronotypes and sleep architecture. These populations provide an evolutionary model to investigate how circadian timing, sleep architecture and homeostatic regulation may be linked.

papers.title: Social information use promotes breeding synchrony but constrains adaptation to rapid environmental changes
papers.abstract: Animals use social information to make decisions, yet how such processes influence predictions in reproductive timing and population adaptation under environmental change remains unclear. While social information can improve decision accuracy through information pooling, spatiotemporal heterogeneity in conditions and patterns of environmental changes creates noise that potentially limits the value of social information use among breeding individuals. Here, we established an evolutionary individual-based model to examine how social and private sensing interact to shape breeding phenology in species distributed across territories with peaked resources and facing annual fluctuations and rapid climate change. We show that when individuals incorporate social information from neighbours, behavioural responses become increasingly synchronised through positive feedback in decision-making. This emergent synchrony helps populations to adapt faster and can increase reproductive output under stable environmental conditions relative to relying only on private information. However, under directional climate change, the same mechanism reduces population responsiveness by constraining variation in individual responses, leading to systematic lag in tracking shifting environmental optima and reduced population reproductive output. Our results demonstrate that social information use can produce a general trade-off at the population level between synchronisation and adaptive flexibility across environmental contexts. Social interaction enhances population performance when environments are either consistent or changing drastically across both spatial and temporal scales. Rather than uniformly improving performance, social interaction may create conditions under which collective behaviour becomes maladaptive when environments change rapidly.

papers.title: Hydrogen sulfide modulation of intrinsic excitability in rat hippocampal CA1 pyramidal cells
papers.abstract: Although traditionally known as a toxic gas, hydrogen sulfide (H2S) is now recognized as a biologically active molecule with modulatory effects on many physiological targets, including the central nervous system. In this context, pyramidal cells of the hippocampus express the H2S-generating enzymes required for its synthesis and local release. Nonetheless, the effects of H2S on the passive and active membrane properties of glutamatergic neurons of the hippocampus remain incompletely characterized. To investigate these effects, we examined how application of an exogenous H2S donor and inhibition of endogenous H2S synthesis shape passive membrane properties, action potential dynamics, firing frequency, and activation of voltage-dependent currents in rat hippocampal CA1 pyramidal cells. Acute exposure to the H2S donor sodium hydrosulfide (NaHS, 200 uM) modified passive membrane integration and action potential dynamics and reduced firing frequency. These functional alterations were associated with decreased amplitude of voltage-dependent inward and outward currents. Western blot analysis confirmed the expression of H2S -producing enzymes (CBS, CSE, and 3-MST) in tissue resected from the CA1 pyramidal cell layer. In contrast to NaHS, treatment with aminooxyacetic acid (AOAA, 100 uM), a nonselective inhibitor of H2S synthesis, produced limited effects on passive membrane properties but increased firing frequency. Collectively, these results indicate that exogenous H2S reduces the intrinsic excitability of hippocampal CA1 pyramidal cells. Thes findings characterize the effect of H2S on membrane properties and voltage-dependent currents that contribute to neuronal firing.
